The growth of AI over the past five years has been truly remarkable. Generative AI (LLM) names like Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude have become part of our daily conversations, and it has become standard practice to write text and generate code on our screens.

In this article, I will explain in an easy-to-understand way the history of conventional microcontroller programming and ROS (Robot Operating System), starting from the question "What is AI anyway?", and why Physical AI is said to be putting an end to (or opening a new era for) the history of robot development!
1. Conventional Robot Control: Programming Microcontrollers
Until now, the foundation of robot development has been "humans writing code (programs) to make microcontrollers like Arduino, ESP32, or STM32 move."
"If the switch is pressed, rotate the servo 90 degrees."
In this way, humans program and describe all conditional branches and operational rules in advance.

The biggest challenge that arises here is that "it can only move exactly as programmed." The moment there is an unexpected step or an unforeseen obstacle rolls in, the robot becomes lost and stops moving, or it malfunctions.
The open-source middleware "ROS (Robot Operating System)" has been used as the standard for robotics for a long time to solve this problem.
"Physical AI" holds the potential to put a complete end to the long-standing problem of "humans having to define every movement and condition."

Simply put, it is 'a technology that gives a body (physical form) to AI (LLMs and image recognition) that previously existed only on screens, allowing it to learn and adapt directly in the physical world.'

For example, in the past, writing a program to 'harvest strawberries of different shapes without crushing them' was an extremely difficult task. However, with Physical AI, by integrating camera footage and tactile sensor data, the robot can learn to grasp any strawberry gently, just as humans learn to adjust their grip through sensation.
